_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Rashi and Tosafot: Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>, matching pipeline/sources. Square brackets are our clarifications.
rashi:a1.1: A gallery built over the eastern gate [of the Temple Mount], which was called Shushan the capital, as explained in Menachot, chapter Shtei HaLeḥem (98a).
rashi:a2.1: When they contracted with the craftsmen to do so many cubits of work for the Temple’s upkeep, they contracted by Moses’ cubit, and the craftsmen did the work by the larger measure, one of the cubits kept in Shushan the capital.
rashi:a2.2: So that they would not benefit from consecrated property. Had they worked by the same measure they had contracted with, they might fall short, since it is impossible to be exact. So they “return” by the larger one.
rashi:a3.1: One would be enough, apart from Moses’ cubit of six handbreadths.
rashi:a3.2: Since that is painstaking work, they contracted by Moses’ cubit and delivered by the one that is larger than it by half a fingerbreadth.
rashi:a3.3: For building a wall, they were paid by Moses’ cubit and delivered by the one that exceeds it by a full fingerbreadth.
rashi:a5.1: If it has no testicles, or has only one testicle, that is a blemish.
rashi:a5.2: Every animal has a separate sac for each testicle: the scrotum is divided down the middle, and you can see it from outside, because the middle is sunken and a deep line shows there.
rashi:a5.3: We read akuzo, as discussed in Eruvin, chapter Keitzad Me’abrin (53b): did we learn akuzo or akuzo [with an alef or with an ayin]? “On its akuz” means on its haunches: one seats the firstborn that seems to have only one testicle on its hindquarters.
rashi:a5.4: He feels around the sac and the loins. If there is a testicle, it will eventually come out; if it does not come out, it is a blemish.
rashi:a5.5: Kesalim [loins]: in Old French, flancs, the flanks.
rashi:a5.6: Rabbi Akiva permitted it: it counts as a blemish, since the testicle was not in its place.
rashi:a6.1: Rabbi Yishmael disputes only the latter clause. The first tanna says that one testicle with two sacs is a blemish, and Rabbi Yishmael comes to say that we know it has two testicles. But on the first clause he agrees: if it has only one sac, it is like one with only one testicle, and is treated like one whose testicles are crushed.
rashi:a8.1: Piran is the name of the village.
rashi:a10.1: Sacrificial animals outside: since it has no blemish, it is still in its sanctity.
rashi:a11.1: Whose thighbone was dislocated: where the sinew has not rotted. If the sinew had rotted it would also be a tereifa, as stated in Chullin, chapter Elu Tereifot (54b): if the hip-socket bone slipped from its place, it is a tereifa, and that applies when the sinew has rotted.
rashi:a11.2: One higher than the other: the hip socket of this thigh has moved up toward the back, higher than the other one.
rashi:a12.1: They taught this only…: that an animal with five or three legs has a blemish and is not a tereifa.
rashi:a12.2: Only where what is missing or extra is a foreleg: the five-legged animal has three forelegs and two hind legs, and the three-legged one has two hind legs and one foreleg. The rules of tereifa do not apply to a foreleg.
rashi:a12.3: It is like a removed limb: an animal whose thigh and its socket were removed is a neveila [carcass]. And we hold that an animal whose legs were cut off above the knee joint is a tereifa, and also that if the hip-socket bone slipped from its place it is a tereifa.
rashi:a13.1: Do not say that they must resemble a donkey’s in every respect: round and not split.
rashi:a13.2: Rather, since they are round like a donkey’s, it is a blemish, because the hooves of a kosher animal are not round.
rashi:a14.1: Kesalei: in Old French, flanc, the flank.
rashi:a14.2: Inside the loin: this is the normal build of the animal. The thigh joins the rump near the loins, not above them on the back of the rump.
rashi:a14.3: Whose thigh is extended: one of its thighs is larger than the other.
rashi:a15.1: Even though it is not conspicuous: the Gemara explains this.
rashi:a16.1: We have heard only of these: the ones mentioned above. And these are the three he added: one whose eye is round, and so on.
rashi:a16.2: Like that of a pig: the Gemara explains this.
rashi:a16.3: Most of the speaking part: that is, the part of the tongue that is free and not attached to the jaw.
rashi:a17.1: On its own account: the fracture itself cannot be seen, but you can tell because the animal limps. The walking of the leg is its “work.”
rashi:a18.1: That it is not its normal way: for an animal’s eye to be round.
rashi:a18.2: She observes for a male: seven days of impurity and thirty-three days of purity.
rashi:a19.1: For a female: fourteen impure days and sixty-six pure ones.
rashi:a19.2: For a male and for a female, stringently: the days of impurity of a female, two weeks, and the days of purity of a male, so that she has only thirty-three days of purity.
rashi:a20.1: What is Rabbi Meir’s reason: for saying that a woman who gives birth to the form of a non-kosher animal has given birth, as with a real child.
rashi:a20.2: Since: it resembles a person in the eyeball.
rashi:a20.3: The black: the black of an animal’s eye is round like a person’s.
rashi:a20.4: The white: the whole setting of the white and the lid is called tzirya, and that is certainly not round like a person’s.
rashi:a21.1: Do not say that it must resemble a pig in every respect, both shafid and paris. Shafid: its mouth is round. Paris: the upper lip and upper cheeks overhang the lower ones. But from my teacher we received the reverse: shafid means its upper cheeks narrow to a point, like a spit [shapud].
rashi:a24.1: What did it teach: what is this incident like, that it says “and there was an incident”?
tosafot:a8.1: In Piran of Beit Menaḥem: Rashi explains that this is the name of the village. But the Tosefta (chapter 4) reads “with the cow [para] of Beit Menaḥem,” like the incident of the cow of Beit Menaḥem whose womb was removed (Sanhedrin 33a).
tosafot:a11.1: Whose thigh was dislocated: Rashi explains it (in Old French, esloisier, dislocated) as a case where the sinew had not rotted, for if it had, it would also be a tereifa, as stated in Chullin (55b). But this is difficult for his explanation, since there is an opinion there that it is a tereifa even if the sinew had not rotted or been severed. Rather, explain that it was dislocated this way from birth; and the same applies to “whose thigh is extended” below.
rashi:b2.1: With regard to a person: that is, a kohen.
rashi:b3.1: Where it contains a bone: if the lower jawbone protrudes beyond the upper one, it is a blemish even in an animal. But where there is no bone, only that the lower lip is long, takes in the upper lip and protrudes beyond it, that is a blemish in a person but not in an animal.
rashi:b4.1: The ear of the kid that was doubled: it has two ears on one side, an ear within an ear.
rashi:b4.2: When it is one bone: they have only one cartilage. The upper cartilage folded into it and joined it below. That is a blemish.
rashi:b4.3: When it does not have its own bone: the cartilages are separate at the top, and it is not a blemish. The reason was not explained to me, and it is not like an animal with five legs, because this ear within an ear is not so noticeable.
rashi:b4.4: Like that of a pig: the Gemara explains this.
rashi:b5.2: Mevulamot: narrow in width. (Rashi adds an Old French gloss.)
rashi:b5.3: If due to the space: it simply lacks room in the mouth, neither in the bone nor in the flesh of the lips. That is not a blemish.
rashi:b5.4: If due to the bone: the lips open well, but the jaws are pressed together so that it cannot open them; when it eats or bleats it widens its lips, and the bone looks like a pouch. That is a blemish. The same for the legs: if they are short due to the space, because the bone and the flesh of the feet are of one measure and not very wide, it is not a blemish; if due to the bone, because the bone is short and the flesh widens below and sticks out, it is a blemish. My teacher read “due to the wind” and explained it as I did, but the wording cannot be corrected; others read “due to the space,” as I explained. Another explanation: “its mouth is balum” means swollen. If it swelled from a passing cause it is not a blemish, since it will heal; if due to the bone, which is very thick, it is a blemish. And in the Tosefta of Bekhorot (4:4) we found: due to the wind, it is not a blemish; due to itself, it is a blemish.
rashi:b5.5: Ḥasḥus: the cartilage of the ear.
rashi:b6.2: Kerikha: round. A lamb’s tail is normally wider than it is thick.
rashi:b7.1: In a kid, two: two joints in the tail is a blemish.
rashi:b8.1: The first clause is the ear of the kid. The latter clause is “that does not have three joints.”
rashi:b9.1: Yabelet, a wart: in Old French, verrue.
rashi:b9.2: Where the bone of its foreleg was damaged: here the blemish is visible. Above (40a) it spoke of a bone that was broken.
rashi:b9.3: The bone of its mouth: the bone in which the teeth are set, above the gums. If it were the gums themselves, even a damaged or worn-down gum would also be a blemish.
rashi:b9.4: By sight: anyone can see that this one is larger than that one.
rashi:b9.5: But not by measurement: if it can be noticed only by measuring, it is not a blemish.
rashi:b9.6: But the Rabbis did not agree with him: this refers to Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:b10.1: Not in the Temple: since it is disqualified from the altar.
rashi:b10.2: Nor in the country: since it is not a full blemish that would allow it to be slaughtered outside.
rashi:b11.1: And how can you understand it: that it is not a blemish?
rashi:b11.2: But a wart is written in the Torah: among the full blemishes (Leviticus 22): “blind, or broken, or maimed, or with a wart.”
rashi:b11.3: On its body: there it is not a full blemish.
rashi:b12.1: But the verse is written without qualification.
rashi:b12.2: Rather: on the body too it is a blemish. The verse, which implies a wart on the body is a blemish, does not contradict the mishna, which implies that it is a full blemish only in the eye while on the body it disqualifies from the altar but does not permit slaughter outside. The verse speaks of a wart that has a bone; our mishna here, in the eye, is a blemish; and the other mishna, on the body, is not a blemish because it has no bone.
rashi:b14.1: And where it has no bone, on the body, it is disqualified? This is asked in surprise.
rashi:b14.2: Taltul: pieces of flesh that hang from the body, like people who have small strips of flesh beside their ears from birth.
rashi:b14.3: Disqualifies a person: if he is a kohen, he is disqualified from the Temple service, since we require one who is “equal to the seed of Aaron.”
rashi:b14.4: Rather, both refer to the eye: this refers to the two mishnayot, not to the verse.
rashi:b15.1: But there are no blemishes in the white: so even in the Temple it may be slaughtered as an offering.
rashi:b15.2: Both: the mishna that says one does not slaughter in the Temple or in the country, and the teaching that there are no blemishes in the white, both speak of a wart in the white. Where it has a hair it is unsightly, and about that the mishna says one slaughters neither in the Temple nor in the country.
rashi:b15.3: And that: the teaching “there are no blemishes in the white” is where the wart has no hair. And our mishna, that it is a full blemish, is in the black, as we established, and also where it has no bone; the verse is where it has a bone. For if our mishna here were where it has a bone, why would it specify “in its eye”?
rashi:b17.1: And the Rabbis, who did not agree with him about the testicles: how much smaller may the other one be and still be fit, in their view?
rashi:b18.1: La’arkov: to the joint of the thigh. The Gemara explains which joint.
rashi:b18.2: All growth of calves: the whole development and normal way of calves is that their tails reach that joint, so anything shorter is a blemish. As they grow, the tails keep stretching further down.
rashi:b18.3: In the middle of the thigh: the Gemara explains this.
tosafot:b5.1: Its mouth is balum: Rashi gave, as a second explanation, “swollen.” His first explanation, that balum means short, is better, since balum is a word for closing up, as in “its nose is balum” below in chapter Mumin Elu (43b), which Rashi explains there as nostrils that are blocked; and as in “one who restrains [bolem] himself during a quarrel” in chapter Kisui HaDam (Chullin 89a).
tosafot:b15.1: But there are no blemishes in the white: although that is disputed above (38b), we already established the mishna there according to the view that there are no blemishes in the white.
tosafot:b15.2: Rather, both refer to the black: that is our reading; we do not read “the white.”
gershom:a1.1: [On the tzitzit baraita of 39b:] Beit Shammai say four fingerbreadths. The braided part is a third of the strand, so the strand is eight fingerbreadths and the whole is three handbreadths, which is a span. From here we learn that tzitzit are a span long, since in Menachot we do not learn how long they are. And in tzitzit we practice like Beit Shammai: four strings and four fingerbreadths of braiding.
gershom:a2.1: Rav Huna [son of Rav Yehoshua] says that the fingerbreadth the Sages spoke of is the fingerbreadth by which the cubit exceeds Moses’ cubit, which is a quarter of the handbreadth of any person.
gershom:a3.1: And Rav Naḥman says it refers to the fingerbreadth in our mishna, between one joint and the next.
gershom:a4.1: Rabbi Akiva says: even though it has two sacs, we do not say it is known that it has two testicles with the second hidden in the belly. Rather, this is how it is examined: one seats the firstborn on its rump, on its tail and haunches, and mashes the sac; if there is another testicle there, it will eventually come out.
gershom:a5.1: And Rabbi Akiva permitted it: since it was mashed and the testicle did not come out, it is a blemish, and it is permitted to eat it.
gershom:a6.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri prohibited it, since the testicle was found.
gershom:a7.1: If it has only one sac, even though it has two testicles, it is as though it has only one testicle. And Rabbi Akiva comes to say, etc.
gershom:a8.1: “An incident with the cow of Beit Menaḥem.” You are destroying the property of Israel: since you forbid eating these animals outside the Temple, there is nothing to do with them but bury them.
gershom:a9.1: Sacrificial animals outside: since it is unblemished, it may be eaten only in Jerusalem. (A later editor’s note: that is, in Temple times it would be eaten in Jerusalem and offered on the altar like any unblemished firstborn.)
gershom:a10.1: It is also a tereifa: since any extra limb is like a removed limb, and we learned that an animal whose legs were cut off from the knee joint upward is a tereifa, because that is where the sinews meet.
gershom:a11.1: The kasul: one of its legs goes in among the loins, and its other leg sits on top of the loin, at the end of the loin.
gershom:a12.1: Whose thigh is extended: it is longer than the other.
gershom:a13.1: Most of the speaking part of its tongue was removed: most of the part of the tongue that is free of the lower palate, the part it can bend upward.
gershom:a14.1: It is not visible from outside, so is it a blemish? We require blemishes that are exposed.
gershom:a15.1: But it is visible on account of its work: you can see it when it walks, and walking is called its work.
gershom:a16.1: Is this to say that it is not its normal way for its eye to be round like a person’s?
gershom:a17.1: She observes for a male and for a female: forty days as for a male, and of the two she keeps fourteen days of impurity, as for a female.
gershom:a18.1: This refers to the black and that to the white: that is, the black of the eye is normally round like a person’s.
gershom:a19.1: Tzirya: the whole opening of the eye. It is not normal for that to be round.
gershom:a21.1: And paris: its lip curves upward like a pig’s.
gershom:a22.1: And the Rabbis disagree with him: since they said, “We did not hear about those.”
gershom:a23.1: But we learned in the chapter below: “his upper lip protrudes,” etc.
gershom:b1.1: But in an animal it is not a blemish.
gershom:b2.1: It is not difficult: this is where there is a bone in its lower lip, and then it is a blemish.
gershom:b4.1: When it is one bone: it has one cartilage and is doubled above. That is a blemish.
gershom:b5.1: Its mouth is balum: very narrow.
gershom:b6.1: And its legs are mevulamot: the hooves are sharp and very tight.
gershom:b7.1: If due to the space: that is, if it is narrow because it does not open it wide, it is not a blemish.
gershom:b8.1: If narrow due to the bone: the bone is very tight and because of that it cannot open its mouth. That is a blemish.
gershom:b12.1: Three is not a blemish, since that is its normal way.
gershom:b13.1: The latter clause, “or that it does not have three joints,” speaks of a lamb.
gershom:b14.1: Or the bone of its mouth was damaged: its jaw.
gershom:b15.1: That one does not slaughter on account of them: one may not slaughter the firstborn in the Temple to offer it, because perhaps it is a blemish.
gershom:b16.1: Nor in the country: because perhaps it is not a blemish, and outside one may slaughter it only on account of a definite blemish.
gershom:b17.1: And one with a wart: this shows that it is not a full blemish.
gershom:b18.1: It is not difficult: the mishna that says one does not slaughter on account of a wart is when it is on the body; the mishna and the verse that count it as a blemish are when it is in the eye. The verse speaks of a wart that has a bone, and a wart on the body with a bone is a blemish. The mishna that says one does not slaughter speaks of one without a bone. In the eye, even without a bone it is a blemish; on the body without a bone it is not a blemish. “But it is disqualified from being offered? Why? It is mere hanging flesh.” Taltul is like a mole of flesh hanging from the skin.
gershom:b19.1: The white: there are no blemishes in the white, so why may one not slaughter it in the Temple?
gershom:b20.1: Rather, both refer to the white. (This is how it was expounded at the kallah, on the Shabbat before the festival.)
gershom:b21.1: This, where it has a hair: a wart in the white is a blemish. It teaches that although other blemishes in the white do not disqualify, if the wart has a hair it disqualifies, and if it has no hair it does not.
gershom:b22.1: By sight but not by measurement: that is, it gives no measure for a large ear the way it gives one for a large eye and a large testicle.
gershom:b23.1: And the Rabbis, who did not agree with him: how much smaller than the other may one testicle be before it is a blemish, if double is not enough?
gershom:b24.1: Arkov: the place of the hip socket.
